chief_complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes
hpi_details: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he has an unusually severe case of strep throat or a bad tonsil abscess.
concerns: He is worried that the huge, painful lumps in his neck might be lymphoma or throat cancer like his father had.
expectations: He hopes to have a rapid throat swab done and receive strong penicillin and numbing throat spray to be able to swallow again.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 92, BP 118/74. Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudates with palatal petechiae, mild splenomegaly on abdominal palpation. Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test positive; CBC shows lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Streptococcal pharyngitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe abdominal pain — could indicate splenic enlargement or rupture risk.
management_principles: Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes

A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 92, BP 118/74. Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudates with palatal petechiae, mild splenomegaly on abdominal palpation. Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test positive; CBC shows lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes.
reference_soap.assessment: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV), confirmed by positive heterophile antibody testing and atypical lymphocytosis; mild splenomegaly noted, warranting contact/sport precautions.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk). Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Infectious Mononucleosis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Infectious Mononucleosis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk)

teaching.one_liner: Epstein-Barr virus infection causing severe sore throat, high fever, and marked cervical lymphadenopathy — contact sports should be avoided due to splenic rupture risk.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain — could indicate splenic enlargement or rupture risk

must_ask.say: How severe is the sore throat?
Are the glands in your neck swollen?
How high has the fever been?
Any pain or fullness in your upper left belly?

history.answer: I've come in because of a terrible sore throat, a high fever, and huge swollen lumps on both sides of my neck.
It started about five days ago with a scratchy throat and tiredness, and it has gotten progressively worse each day.
The throat pain is severe, around an eight out of ten, and it feels equally intense across both sides.
Swallowing solids hurts intensely, but I can still swallow liquids and my own saliva without drooling.
My breathing is normal with no noisy breathing, though my voice sounds a bit muffled because my throat is so swollen.
I can open my mouth completely without any stiffness or spasm in my jaw.
Yes, I've had high fevers reaching nearly 39 degrees Celsius along with severe chills and night sweats.
No cough, no runny nose, no nasal congestion, and no redness in my eyes.
Both sides of my neck, particularly toward the back, have huge swollen glands that feel tender when touched.
No, I haven't noticed any rashes on my skin.
I feel completely exhausted and drained of energy, and I can barely get out of bed.
I have felt a dull fullness and mild discomfort under my ribs on the upper left side, but no sharp or unbearable pain.
No, the pain stays in my throat and does not radiate up into my ears.
A colleague at work was out with a severe viral illness and swollen glands a few weeks ago, but no one at home is sick.
I haven't had severe tonsillitis or strep throat since I was a teenager.
No acid reflux, heartburn, or frequent throat clearing.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my partner and have had no new sexual partners or oral sex with anyone else.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions, diabetes, or immune system problems.
I thought maybe I caught a really vicious case of strep throat or developed an abscess on my tonsils.
I'm really worried that these huge lumps in my neck might actually be lymphoma, which my father died of.
I have no past medical problems and have always been healthy.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, only over-the-counter acetaminophen for the fever.
I have no known allergies to medications, including penicillin.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend, but I haven't had anything to drink since getting sick.
I work as an office manager and live in an apartment with my partner.
My parents are in their late sixties and both healthy, with no history of blood disorders or chronic illnesses.

exam.finding: Appears fatigued and acutely ill, but sitting comfortably without respiratory distress, tripod positioning, or drooling.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 38.9 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Bilateral tonsillar enlargement with thick exudates and palatal petechiae; the uvula is midline without peritonsillar fullness or asymmetry.
Marked bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy with mild tenderness; anterior cervical lymph nodes are also enlarged.
Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness over the left upper quadrant, but no guarding or rebound tenderness.
Palpable spleen tip extending approximately 2 cm below the left costal margin; liver edge is non-tender and not enlarged.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with good air entry and no crackles, wheezes, or stridor.
No erythematous, maculopapular, petechial, or sandpaper-like rashes noted on the body.
